title: Where does the pattern of nines lead us?
description: A pattern begins at the largest three digit number and adds one again and again, until the boxes reach the smallest six digit number. Keeko then raises a hand to ask where a number as big as a lakh turns up in real life, and the book's cricket stadium answers it.
teaching_notes: One idea: adding one to a number made only of nines gives the smallest number with one more digit. Ask the class to say how many nines the largest number of each size has before adding one. Watch for students who add one to the last digit only and forget that every nine rolls over.

source: Fill in the pattern: the largest 3-digit number is 999; give the smallest and largest 4-digit and 5-digit numbers and the smallest 6-digit number
video_script.why: The child can count and read thousands but has not yet seen where the six digit numbers begin.
video_script.substitution: A number made of nines rolls over to zeros when one is added, and a one appears in front.
video_script.anchor: Starting from 999, find the smallest and largest numbers with four, five and six digits
video_script.payoff_line: The smallest six digit number is one lakh
maths_rules: 999 + 1 = 1000, the smallest 4-digit number; the largest 4-digit number is 9999
9999 + 1 = 10,000, the smallest 5-digit number; the largest 5-digit number is 99,999
99,999 + 1 = 1,00,000, the smallest 6-digit number, read as one lakh
video_script.design: One idea: a number made of nines rolls over to zeros when one is added, and a one appears in front. Keeko's raised hand ends the video with the book's own cricket stadium. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

<bookmark mark='m3'/>Adding one each time, which is the smallest six digit number?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Look at the largest three digit number. Every digit in it is a nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A nine is a full place, so one more makes it roll over to zero.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The place next to it then gets one more, and a new place may open at the front.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the largest three digit number is nine hundred ninety nine, and we add one each time.

beats.on_screen: To find: the smallest and largest 4-digit and 5-digit numbers, and the smallest 6-digit number

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to fill the boxes. Find the smallest and largest numbers with four and five digits. Then find the smallest with six digits.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 999 + 1 = 1000, the smallest 4-digit number; the largest 4-digit number is 9999
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, add one to nine hundred ninety nine. We get one thousand, the smallest four digit number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The largest four digit number has four nines, nine thousand nine hundred ninety nine.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 9999 + 1 = 10,000, the smallest 5-digit number; the largest 5-digit number is 99,999
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, add one again, and we get ten thousand, the smallest five digit number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The largest five digit number has five nines, ninety nine thousand nine hundred ninety nine.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 99,999 + 1; the five nines roll over to zeros and a 1 arrives in front, making a number with six digits

marks.m2: the five nines roll to zeros and a 1 arrives in front

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, add one to ninety nine thousand nine hundred ninety nine.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>All five nines roll over to zeros, and a one arrives in front, so six digits are needed.

beats.on_screen: Answer: the smallest 6-digit number is 1,00,000, read as one lakh; the last box of the pattern is filled

marks.m1: 1,00,000 is written in the last box and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The smallest six digit number is one lakh, a one followed by five zeros.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the filled pattern
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us see where such a big number turns up.

beats.on_screen: a drawn cricket stadium full of seats; a label says more than one lakh seats
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko wonders where a lakh is found around us.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Your book says the cricket stadium in Ahmedabad has a seating capacity of more than one lakh.
